data.title: A Channel-Boosted Multi-Agent System with Iterative Consultation for Document Sensitivity Classification
data.author: Aleesha Zainab, Asifullah Khan, Muhammad Ahmed Khalid, Faheem Ullah Khan
data.summary: Organizations in critical national infrastructure sectors must assess heterogeneous documents for sensitivity before routing or storage. Manual assessment is slow, inconsistent, and unscalable. Extending our prior leakage-controlled benchmark, BERT established the top single-encoder baseline (89.14% accuracy, 89.33% F1-score under 5-fold cross-validation on the Strategic 16K corpus). However, transformer baselines suffer from a structural limitation: fixed input length truncation discards evidence beyond the retained window-precisely where sensitive cables tend to be longest. We present Channel-Boosted MAS (CB-MAS) and instantiate it as IC-MAS (Iterative Consultation Multi-Agent System) to solve this without long-context computational costs. A Channel Critic Agent learns document-adaptive trust weights governing Gated Channel Boosting between two first-window encoders, while paired Consultation Agents iteratively exchange belief states to reconcile evidence from the beginning and end of long documents. IC-MAS holds computation constant regardless of document length by reconciling fixed windows in a compact representation space. Ablation studies show critic-controlled Channel Boosting provides the bulk of accuracy gains, while consultation recovers recall without precision collapse. Critic-Controlled Gated Channel Boosting with Max-Pool fusion and Blackboard Adaptive Consultation achieves 90.72% accuracy, 91.23% F1-score, 92.01% sensitive recall, and 90.46% sensitive precision, using about 54% less average computation than a fixed-round baseline. Gains over the single-encoder baseline are statistically significant (McNemar's test, p less than 0.000001; paired t-test). We include LIME/SHAP explainability, multi-agent evaluation, and an honest accounting of limitations.

oai:arXiv.org:2609.22212v3.label: A Channel-Boosted Multi-Agent System with Iterative Consultation for Document Sensitivity Classification

data.title: PACE-dLLM: Elastic Block Decoding via Confidence Cliff Estimation for Diffusion Language Models
data.author: Xiaocheng Lu, Shuhan Guo, Ziyue Ma, Jie Zhang, Jian Liu, Jingcai Guo, Haoxuan Che, Song Guo
data.summary: Diffusion language models (dLLMs), such as LLaDA and Dream, have become competitive with autoregressive (AR) LLMs in generation quality while supporting native parallel decoding. A standard acceleration strategy is block-wise decoding, where each forward pass predicts a block of length B and commits high-confidence tokens. Confidence-threshold commitment adapts which tokens are accepted, but a fixed B still constrains the prediction scope. Existing horizon policies use manually chosen sizes, volatility statistics, or candidate-boundary scores. We instead use the model's own per-step confidence: in-window confidence typically follows a context-dependent cliff, providing a direct signal for adapting the look-ahead horizon. In this work, we propose PACE-dLLM, which refits this parametric cliff periodically in closed form, sets the next horizon at a shared confidence anchor, and retains confidence-threshold token commitment. Under a saturated-yield abstraction with iid, policy-independent monotone profiles, the oracle horizon is the smallest attaining maximal per-pass yield and improves the asymptotic forward-pass rate when fixed blocks undershoot it with positive probability. On four reasoning and code benchmarks across two open-source dLLM backbones, PACE-dLLM achieves the best average accuracy among the evaluated decoders on both backbones, with average throughput speedups of 5.23x on LLaDA and 3.06x on Dream (up to 8.52x on LLaDA MATH) over the unaccelerated semi-AR baseline, advancing the quality-throughput Pareto frontier.

oai:arXiv.org:2609.26249v2.label: PACE-dLLM: Elastic Block Decoding via Confidence Cliff Estimation for Diffusion Language Models

data.title: Enhancing Assessment of Self-Consistency in LLM Explanations using Perturbation Strength
data.author: Phuong Q. Le, Kemal Kurniawan, Jey Han Lau
data.summary: Prior work has examined the self-consistency of LLM-generated explanations using surface-level perturbation methods. However, the strength of these perturbations is not explicitly measured and controlled. In this work, we propose an LLM-as-a-judge approach to measure perturbation strength in a unified manner across input and CoT perturbations. We then evaluate the self-consistency in explanations generated from various LLMs under controlled strength conditions, ensuring a fair comparison across perturbation types. Experiments show that our proposed LLM-based perturbation strength measure outperforms other embedding- and probability-based approaches and that input perturbations generally affect LLMs more strongly than CoT perturbations. Our work suggests that judgments about a model's self-consistency is fair only within the same perturbation type.

oai:arXiv.org:2609.30849v2.label: Enhancing Assessment of Self-Consistency in LLM Explanations using Perturbation Strength

data.title: Rewarding Novel Deductions: Solver-guided Process Supervision for Logical Reasoning
data.author: Muhammad Asif Ali, Wenqing Wang, Huan Wang, Mohammad Raza
data.summary: Logical reasoning remains a major challenge for large language models (LLMs), particularly on structured problems that require precise constraint tracking, consistency preservation, and multi-step deduction. This challenge is especially acute for small-scale LLMs, which are more prone to producing inconsistent, redundant, or brittle reasoning trajectories. Existing approaches for improving logical reasoning largely optimize for final-answer correctness, providing only weak supervision over the intermediate reasoning process. In this work, we propose SPRING: (Solver-guided Process Rewards for Novel LogIcal ReasoNing Step Generation). SPRING uses an SMT solver as a training-time verifier of intermediate reasoning steps to provide process-level supervision. It introduces the notion of a novel reasoning step, namely, a step that is logically valid, consistent with the evolving reasoning state, and not already implied by previously accepted non-contradictory deductions. Based on this solver-based assessment, it designs process rewards that encourage novel inferential progress while penalizing contradictory and uninformative reasoning steps. Evaluation across three logical reasoning benchmarks: ZebraLogic, AR-LSAT, and Knights and Knaves, and four LLMs shows that SPRING consistently outperforms base LLMs, outcome-only reward baselines, and Logic-LM. On ZebraLogic, SPRING improves puzzle accuracy by up to 49.71 and 15.43 points over the base LLM and strongest outcome-only baseline, respectively. On AR-LSAT, it improves overall accuracy by up to 64.43 and 11.39 percentage points over the base LLM and strongest outcome-only baseline, respectively. On Knights and Knaves, SPRING achieves up to 93.14 puzzle accuracy and 96.05 person accuracy.

data.title: Measuring Collapse and Correction in Homogeneous-Panel LLM Debate
data.author: Xin Li, Mengbing Liu, Chau Yuen
data.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) debate is often evaluated by whether final answers improve, but a changed answer is not necessarily a better one: the same discussion can correct an initially wrong majority or collapse an initially correct one. Standard final-accuracy evaluations conflate these opposing transitions. We introduce an auditable protocol for homogeneous debate on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) that records each run as a transition ledger over collapse, correction, onset, and signed intervention utility. On 6,925 MMLU-Pro debates, the protocol records 253 collapses together with the corrections that offset them, and the correction side changes how interventions should be judged. Replay experiments reveal the central tradeoff: freezing every debate prevents 251 collapses but loses 804 corrections under equal weights, and a leave-one-model-out probe-gated freeze that is tuned for net utility never fires, so collapse prevention alone can recommend the wrong policy. A compact pre-debate 8-probe screen is a triage signal: its unadjusted family-level association with conditional-collapse risk is high (G=7, Spearman $\rho$ = 0.893, exact two-sided p = 0.0123), but initial-majority accuracy is a close comparator ($\rho$ = -0.821; family partial $\rho$ = 0.767, p = 0.0877), so we do not treat it as calibrated or capability-adjusted prediction. Round-level traces localize many collapses to the first debate round, where early disagreement can precede both collapses and corrections. Reasoning-mode models, including one model at two reasoning-effort levels, also show both collapses and corrections. We release replayable schemas, coders, audits, cost cards, and zero-API rebuild scripts so future model rows can be compared under the same denominators and signed utility ledger.

data.title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
data.author: An-Sheng Jhang
data.summary: We measure LLM probability updates on $\delta$-SNLI premise-hypothesis pairs across the Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) family. Separate calls elicit priors and posteriors; directional movement s signs changes by the annotated direction. We cross stated vs. reported wording with Direct single estimates (D0) vs. Multi-Candidate Weighted elicitation (MCW; five weighted estimates, V0, weighted mean M_W). Frozen formal tests cover 15 configurations (23,400 planned units): 3 primary (Qwen3-8B thinking off, OLMo-2-7B, gpt-6.1-sol via codex; 6,600), 4 CLI-harnessed configurations (gpt-oss-120b, claude-sonnet-5.5, gemini-3.8-flash low/high; dnli-agy; 5,600), and 8 un-harnessed REST API configurations (dnli-api; 11,200). We add a 20-configuration, 8-provider dev ladder (3B-550B; 6,000 units) and a 2-model OpenAI 1+1+4 ablation of D0, Direct-CoT (D_CoT), MCW (V0), and Multi-Candidate Unweighted (MCU; V2 / M_U; 1,800 calls). All 15 reject H1 (s = +16.1 to +28.9 points) and H4a (endpoint reduction +0.065 to +0.391); 13 reject H2 (+2.0 to +8.9 points), except gpt-oss-120b (+0.9) and sf:qwen3.5-4b (-0.64). In 14 of 15 formal configurations, readouts obey Top-1 > MCW (M_W) > MCU (M_U). On 120 common pairs, API Qwen3 tracks local Qwen3 (H1 +18.72 vs. +18.90; H4a +0.265 vs. +0.254; H2 +3.78 vs. +1.67; H4b -9.03 vs. -6.70); local H2 rejects on all 240 pairs (+1.97), not this subset. API Gemma 31B (formal H4b -2.85, Top-1 +0.64; spread -13.3% / +7.6%) and Groq gpt-oss-120b (dev -4.15, +0.40; -18.4% / +12.2%) show small MCW costs and stated narrowing/reported widening without CLI harnesses. In OpenAI ablations, D_CoT keeps numeric-token entropy <1 bit; MCU (V2) shows smaller movement loss but halves spread and $\Delta H_2$ vs. MCW (V0). Because $\delta$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about appropriate update magnitude. Code/data: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

data.title: Polarity Blindness in LLM Safety: A Systematic Study of Negation, Antonym Substitution, and Adversarial Framing
data.author: Diego Miguel Lozano, Erik Derner, Juan Antonio P\'erez-Ortiz, Nuria Oliver
data.summary: Negation remains a persistent challenge for language models across NLP tasks and modalities. We show that this weakness can undermine LLM safety guardrails through a structural vulnerability we term polarity blindness: the failure to recognize harmful intent after polarity-altering linguistic transformations. We study two forms of polarity inversion: grammatical negation and antonym replacement, and use synonym replacement as a polarity-preserving control. We further test whether an adversarial textual wrapper amplifies these failures. Using a 260-prompt benchmark across 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and 3 languages (English, Spanish, Czech), stratified by harmfulness potential and evaluated on a validated 0-5 harm scale, we find that polarity blindness affects most evaluated models, with mean harm scores reaching 4.12 for the most vulnerable model. The effect persists across typologically differing negation systems, suggesting that polarity blindness reflects a broader limitation in semantic robustness rather than a language- or grammar-specific failure.

data.title: Bilingual Language Models Capture Cross-Linguistic Influence in Second-Language Reading
data.author: Abderrahmane Issam, Irene E. Winther, Stefan L. Frank
data.summary: While monolingual language model (LM) surprisal is widely established as a predictor of reading times, it cannot capture the non-native (L2) reading dynamics that are shaped by the reader's first language (L1). In this work, we investigate whether the cross-lingual transfer within bilingual models aligns with human L1-driven biases during L2 reading. We evaluate bilingual models on eye-tracking data of readers from 12 diverse L1 backgrounds reading English texts. To isolate L1-specific transfer, we compare bilingual models trained on an L1 that matches the readers' L1 background to both a monolingual English baseline and bilingual models trained on other L1s. We demonstrate that matching the readers' L1 improves the prediction of L2 reading times. This predictive advantage is concentrated in late-stage eye-tracking measures, modulated by L1-L2 script overlap, and peaks among intermediate-proficiency readers. These findings provide evidence that bilingual LMs capture aspects of cross-linguistic influence, and that such influence is present in L2 reading behavior.

data.title: Machine-Readable Operator Manuals over the ISO 11783 Network for Offline, Multilingual LLM Assistance
data.author: Timo Oksanen, Julius Gun
data.summary: If agricultural machinery is to support intelligent, offline assistance, then the system must access technical documentation dynamically. In this paper, the Semantic Synchronization of operator manuals over ISO 11783-based CAN buses is analyzed, defined as the process that brings the local knowledge base of a tractor-side assistant into agreement with the operator manual of the connected implement. Data transfer performance was benchmarked using Markdown, JSON, and XML; various open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) were also evaluated in cross-lingual query tasks. The automatic evaluation of the answers was validated against four human raters. A complete manual was transferred over a physical ISO 11783 network in 31 to 89 s, depending on format and transport settings, which is comparable to the object pool upload that operators already wait for at the first coupling of an implement. Markdown produced the smallest files, while the question-answering performance was comparable across the three formats for most models. With retrieval-augmented generation, locally run models answered most questions on the English manual correctly, with no advantage of the largest model over 7B and 8B models, but performed worse on the five other language editions. Keyword retrieval failed across languages, whereas semantic retrieval provided the cross-lingual capability. The exchange requires only a new parameter group that uses the existing request and transport mechanisms of ISO 11783, which makes it a candidate for standardization. The study is a proof of concept with inference on PC-grade hardware; deployment on embedded agricultural hardware remains future work.

data.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
data.author: Harshavardhan Abichandani, Penny Chong, Atin Ghosh, Daniel Dahlmeier
data.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently across independent runs from identical states. They may call different tools, produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies.This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and 50.5% on ToolSandbox. Across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5 models, RSD reduces AUC CV in seven out of eight model-benchmark settings, while improving the final task progress in all eight settings.

data.title: DynEdit: Dynamic Entropy-Guided Sequential Editing for Large Language Models
data.author: Jinhu Fu, Yan Bai, Yihang Lou, Li Sun, Jiahong Wu, Xiangxiang Chu, Sen Su
data.summary: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated or incorrect knowledge in large language models without full retraining. Existing parameter-editing methods remain limited for long-sequence knowledge: single-point editors provide insufficient coverage for extended targets, while fixed chunk-based editors distribute editing effort uniformly across rigid predefined windows, failing to prioritize difficult, information-dense tokens. In this work, we show that token entropy is closely associated with both editing difficulty and semantic importance: high-entropy regions are harder to edit and often contain key factual content. Motivated by this observation, we propose DynEdit, a dynamic framework for long-sequence knowledge editing. DynEdit uses token-level entropy to guide non-uniform sliding, increasing the coverage of difficult high-entropy regions, and further applies entropy-guided token-level optimization to strengthen updates on information-dense tokens within each editing window. Experiments on three benchmarks and two backbone models show that DynEdit consistently outperforms competitive baselines across diverse long-form editing settings, achieving gains of up to +14.0 BLEU points on challenging paraphrase queries and near-saturated semantic scores on several diverse knowledge domains.

data.title: English Calibration Erodes Lithuanian in Expert-Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
data.author: Tomas Rasymas, Povilas Kvedaras
data.summary: Expert pruning compresses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models by removing the experts that a calibration set marks as unimportant. Studies of high-resource languages largely find that English calibration transfers well to other languages. We test this for Lithuanian: we pruned four MoE models with REAP, removing 25% or 50% of the experts with English, Lithuanian or mixed calibration, and evaluated both languages on reading comprehension, translation and language modelling. English calibration does not transfer to Lithuanian: at 25% pruning, English comprehension fell by a median of 1.7 points but Lithuanian by 21.4. The transfer is asymmetric. Lithuanian calibration removed most of the Lithuanian loss and never significantly hurt English comprehension, which was on average 2.5 points better than under English calibration; only English language modeling got slightly worse. Routing suggests why: in the last layers, Lithuanian sends 55-72% of its expert selections to just eight experts, against 19-39% for English, and English calibration removes some of these experts. Compressed models should be calibrated, and evaluated, in every language they must serve.

data.title: ChartHal: A Fine-grained Framework Evaluating Hallucination of Large Vision Language Models in Chart Understanding
data.author: Xingqi Wang, Yiming Cui, Xin Yao, Shijin Wang, Guoping Hu, Xiaoyu Qin
data.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable progress, yet hallucination remains a critical barrier, particularly in chart understanding, which requires sophisticated perceptual and cognitive abilities as well as rigorous factual accuracy. While prior work has investigated hallucinations and chart comprehension independently, their intersection remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ChartHal, a benchmark that features a fine-grained taxonomy of hallucination scenarios in chart understanding, along with a human-validated dataset of 1,062 samples. Our evaluation shows that state-of-the-art LVLMs suffer from severe hallucinations on ChartHal, including proprietary models such as GPT-5 and o4-mini, which achieve only 34.46% and 22.79% accuracy, respectively. Further analysis reveals that questions involving information absent from or contradictory to charts are especially likely to trigger hallucinations, underscoring the urgent need for more robust mitigation strategies. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ymcui/ChartHal

data.title: More Than Meets the Eye? Uncovering the Reasoning-Planning Disconnect in Training Vision-Language Driving Models
data.author: Xurui Song, Shuo Huai, JingJing Jiang, Jiayi Kong, Jun Luo
data.summary: Vision-Language Model (VLM) driving agents promise explainable end-to-end autonomy by first producing natural-language reasoning and then predicting trajectory planning. However, whether planning is causally driven by this reasoning remains a critical but unverified assumption. To investigate this, we build DriveMind, a large-scale driving Visual Question Answering corpus with plan-aligned Chain-of-Thought (CoT), automatically generated from nuPlan. Our data generation process converts sensors and annotations into structured inputs and, crucially, separates priors from to-be-reasoned signals, enabling clean information ablations. Using DriveMind, we train representative VLM agents with Supervised Fine-Tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization and evaluate them with nuPlan's metrics. Our results, unfortunately, indicate a consistent causal disconnect in reasoning-planning: removing ego/navigation priors causes large drops in planning scores, whereas removing CoT produces only minor changes. Attention analysis further shows that planning primarily focuses on priors rather than the CoT. Based on this evidence, we propose the Reasoning-Planning Decoupling Hypothesis, positing that the training-yielded reasoning is an ancillary byproduct rather than a causal mediator. To enable efficient diagnosis, we introduce a novel, training-free probe that measures an agent's reliance on priors by evaluating its planning robustness against minor input perturbations. In summary, we provide the community with a new dataset and a diagnostic tool to evaluate the causal fidelity of future models.

data.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
data.author: Felipe Valencia-Clavijo
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied as behavioral subjects (e.g., synthetic participants or users) and decision systems (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge), yet it remains unclear how observed cognitive biases relate to changes in model output probabilities. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, provides a useful test case. Prior research largely relies on generated responses, leaving distributional effects and input-field contributions less explored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis examining how numerical anchors shift distributions over candidate outputs, using alternative questions and anchor pairs alongside a positive control to reduce reliance on potentially memorized stimuli; (2) exact Banzhaf-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor contributions to log-probabilities; and (3) an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal predominantly positive behavioral anchoring effects, varying substantially across models. Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B achieve the highest ABSS rankings, whereas other models exhibit weaker behavioral-attributional alignment despite sometimes showing substantial behavioral shifts. Attributional effects also vary across prompts, indicating that behavioral anchoring does not necessarily imply stronger anchor-field contributions. These findings raise questions about LLM reliability as synthetic participants and potential vulnerabilities to numerical cues in automated evaluation and decision-making. More broadly, the framework connects behavioral science with explainable AI, particularly interpretability, and AI safety, providing a reproducible approach to investigating cognitive-bias-like effects in LLMs.

data.title: The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs
data.author: Craig Dickson
data.summary:
Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). While all tested models were susceptible to emergent misalignment, some models showed more resistance than others. Specifically the Qwen-2.5 family proved to be relatively resistant, while GPT-4o exhibited the strongest misalignment. In this paper we evaluate if current-generation open-weights models exhibit similar resistance to the Qwen-2.5 family and measure misalignment robustness over a range of model architectures and scales.
We replicate the effect across nine modern open-weights models (Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, 1B-32B parameters). Models fine-tuned on insecure code generation show a 0.74% misalignment rate (compared to 0.07% for base models), matching the lower end of prior open-model results but dramatically lower than GPT-4o's 20%.
We identify a critical format-dependent vulnerability: requiring JSON output doubles misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts (0.96% vs 0.42%), an effect concentrated in the Gemma 3 family (1.43% vs 0.22%) and not significant in Qwen 3 (0.72% vs 0.59%). This suggests that structural constraints may bypass safety training by reducing the model's 'degrees of freedom' to refuse.
These findings confirm emergent misalignment as a reproducible phenomenon in modern open-weights models, with rates substantially lower than observed in proprietary systems.

data.title: ChemBART: Pre-training a Reaction Language Model for Comprehensive Synthesis Planning
data.author: Kenan Li, Yijian Zhang, Jin Wang, Haipeng Gan, Zeying Sun, Xiaoguang Lei, Hao Dong
data.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated transformative potential across diverse fields. However, in computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP), current LLM methodologies are often restricted to single-molecule representations, limiting their application to isolated, single-task scenarios such as precursor prediction. Addressing this gap, we present ChemBART, a BART-based language model that adopts a reaction-centric pre-training strategy. By leveraging a mask-filling pre-training task on holistic reaction expressions (Reactant > Reagent > Product), ChemBART effectively solves a variety of chemical problems, including precursor/reagent generation, temperature-yield regression, and molecular property classification. The reaction-centric pre-training further enables the integration of ChemBART with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) for multi-step synthesis route design, where the model serves to optimize the policy and value functions within a reinforcement learning framework. Beyond single-molecule pre-trained LLMs that are constrained to specific applications, ChemBART unifies diverse chemical tasks to facilitate synthesis planning with comprehensive implementation information. Most significantly, the proposed multi-step synthesis routes and reaction conditions were validated in the wet lab, confirming the discovery of shorter synthetic pathways with a >20% yield improvement over established literature benchmarks. Our work highlights the potential of reaction-focused pre-training and showcases the broad utility of ChemBART in closing the loop between in silico prediction and wet-lab synthesis.

data.title: LAMaS: A Modular Platform for Learning Low-Latency Multi-Agent Orchestration
data.author: Xi Shi, Mengxin Zheng, Qian Lou
data.summary: In a multi-agent system (MAS), removing an expensive agent call can save tokens without making the answer arrive sooner: latency depends on the longest chain of dependent calls. We present Latency-Aware Multi-agent System (LAMaS), a modular platform for learning low-latency orchestration. A framework can send a query to LAMaS and receive an answer and execution trace, or keep its own graph builder and use the platform's latency-optimized orchestration layer. During training, the layer gives operators on the critical path the greatest latency penalty while targeting a floor on expected accuracy. During inference, a lightweight controller uses partial results to decide whether to skip work that has yet to start. Across four benchmarks, LAMaS reduces end-to-end latency by over 50% relative to the evaluated learning-based MAS baselines while maintaining competitive or better accuracy. GDesigner and AgentDropout retain their graph builders and train the controller on their own traces; both achieve lower latency across the same benchmarks.

data.title: Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion LLMs with Entropy-Guided Step Selection and Stepwise Advantages
data.author: Vishnu Teja Kunde, Fatemeh Doudi, Mahdi Farahbakhsh, Dileep Kalathil, Krishna Narayanan, Jean-Francois Chamberland
data.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been effective for post-training autoregressive (AR) language models, but extending these methods to diffusion language models (DLMs) is challenging due to intractable sequence-level likelihoods. Existing approaches therefore rely on surrogate likelihoods or heuristic approximations, which can introduce bias and obscure the sequential structure of denoising. We formulate diffusion-based sequence generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process over the denoising trajectory and derive an exact, unbiased policy gradient that decomposes over denoising steps and is expressed in terms of intermediate advantages, without requiring explicit evaluation of the sequence likelihood. To obtain a practical and compute-efficient estimator, we (i) select denoising steps for policy updates via an entropy-guided approximation bound, and (ii) estimate intermediate advantages using a one-step denoising reward naturally provided by the diffusion model, avoiding costly multi-step rollouts. Experiments on coding and logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art results, with strong competitive performance on mathematical reasoning, outperforming existing RL post-training approaches for DLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/vishnutez/egspo-dllm-rl.

data.title: Focus Matters: Attention-Value Dynamics for Efficient Hallucination Mitigation in Vision-Language Models
data.author: Sohyeon Kim, Sang Yeon Yoon, Kyeongbo Kong
data.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved impressive progress in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain prone to object hallucinations, generating descriptions of objects that are not present in the input image. In this work, we investigate hallucination from the perspective of attention-value dynamics inside LVLM vision encoders. We identify a consistent three-phase structure of visual processing---diffusion, focus, and rediffusion---and show that the focus phase is where attention most clearly separates strongly and weakly supported visual tokens. However, low attention does not necessarily imply negligible downstream influence: low-attention tokens in the focus phase can still exert non-negligible value-side influence on the attention output relative to their small attention mass. Through controlled phase-wise value interventions, we find that hallucination behavior is particularly sensitive to the value content of low-attention tokens during this phase. Replacing or neutralizing these values reduces hallucination metrics while largely preserving grounded object evidence. A token-level teacher-forcing analysis further shows that the intervention reduces the probability of hallucinated object tokens with much smaller effects on ground-truth object tokens. In addition, Visual Attention Ratio (VAR) analysis shows that focus-phase intervention is accompanied by increased attention to visual tokens during decoding. Based on these observations, we instantiate a simple training-free inference-time intervention that replaces focus-phase low-attention values with an image-level mean value vector using statistics from a single forward pass. Experiments across multiple LVLM backbones demonstrate that this analysis-derived intervention reduces object hallucination with negligible additional runtime and remains compatible with existing inference-time mitigation methods.

oai:arXiv.org:2604.03556v2.label: Focus Matters: Attention-Value Dynamics for Efficient Hallucination Mitigation in Vision-Language Models

data.title: Measuring What Tool-Using LLM Agents Actually Do: Structured Validation, Causal Error Propagation, and Fabricated Tool Use
data.author: Bhaskar Gurram
data.summary: Tool-using agents built on large language models (LLMs) are usually scored by comparing the final answer with a reference text, using a string heuristic or an LLM judge. This is unreliable when the references describe the task rather than its answer. We replace it with a deterministic validator that checks the tools called, the executed parameters, the resulting state, and whether the values in the answer are supported by the correct tool observations. We re-scored 33,583 traces from 13 agents on simulated calendar, weather, medical and retail tools. The simulator reproduced all 10,396 logged observations, and the gold observations supported the validator in 16 of 18 disagreements with a three-annotator majority (the annotators in none). The instrument changes conclusions: on the same 306 traces, Gemini-2.0-Flash scores 63.4% under the substring heuristic and 5.6% under the validator. In a paired design (same task and model, with and without one schema-valid wrong argument injected into the first tool call), the error rate rises from 52.4% to 74.5% (+22.0 percentage points, 95% CI 18.4-25.5; 1,085 pairs, 7 models), and by 44.7 points (38.4-51.0) where the corrupted call executed without errors. An LLM-judge ensemble estimates +2.5 points on the same pairs. Agents also report tool results without executing any call, in 0-42.5% of traces depending on the model (rule-based lower bounds), largely because the harness accepts an action and a final answer in one completion. A rule-based runtime monitor costs about 7 microseconds per trace but reduces wrong answers mainly by abstaining.

data.title: Verifier-Backed Hard Problem Generation for Mathematical Reasoning
data.author: Yuhang Lai, Jiazhan Feng, Yee Whye Teh, Ning Miao
data.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capability in solving scientific and mathematical problems, yet they struggle to produce valid and challenging novel problems -- an essential component for advancing LLM training and enabling autonomous scientific research. Existing problem generation approaches either depend on expensive human expert involvement or adopt naive self-play paradigms, which frequently yield invalid problems due to reward hacking. This work introduces VHG, a verifier-backed hard problem generation framework built upon three-party self-play. By integrating an independent verifier into the conventional setter-solver duality, our design constrains the setter's reward to be jointly determined by problem validity (evaluated by the verifier) and difficulty (assessed by the solver). We instantiate two verifier variants: a Hard symbolic verifier and a Soft LLM-based verifier, with evaluations conducted on indefinite integral tasks and general mathematical reasoning tasks. Experimental results show that VHG substantially outperforms all baseline methods by a clear margin. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/VHG.

data.title: A Communication-Theoretic Framework for LLM Agents: Cost-Aware Adaptive Reliability
data.author: Hamed Omidvar, Vahideh Akhlaghi
data.summary: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) rely on reliability techniques such as retry, majority voting, and self-consistency developed in parallel rather than within a common analytical framework. We observe that an LLM sampled at temperature $T$ is a discrete stochastic channel $p(y \mid x)$ in the sense of Shannon's coding theory, and use this identity as the entry point for such a framework. Each of these techniques is a special case of one of six classical reliability operators: diversity combining, hybrid retransmission, iterative generator-critic decoding, rateless sampling, structured redundant verification, and difficulty-adaptive routing. Within the framework we give two closed-form results, a noise-variance threshold above which uniform averaging beats quality-weighted averaging and a contractivity criterion for generator-critic refinement, and turn each into a design rule checkable before committing compute. We further introduce a cost-aware semantic-nearest-neighbor router whose single Lagrangian knob traverses the quality-cost frontier without retraining. Across six local and cloud channel configurations, no fixed model-technique-budget choice dominates. On a 300-item hard split of MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval, the router occupies the empirical Pareto frontier: at matched quality its normalized cost is $\approx$56% lower than the best fixed technique, and at matched cost it improves quality by $\approx$7% (26% over single-shot decoding). Judge-free grading of 6,900 outputs confirms that the judge tracks correctness at the item level and that the router's advantage over a fixed policy persists at most cost settings; with internal reasoning enabled, the gain of external refinement shrinks but remains significant for our incremental-redundancy operator. These results argue for consolidating reliability techniques into a single tunable layer informed by channel coding.

data.title: Do Semantic Distance Tests Actually Predict Creativity in LLMs? Evidence for Jagged Creativity
data.author: Samuel Schapiro, Alexi Gladstone, Jonah Black, Heng Ji
data.summary: Measuring the creativity of large language models (LLMs) is essential for designing methods that can improve creativity and for enhancing our scientific understanding of this ability. To accomplish this, it has become common in recent years to administer semantic distance tests of human creativity to LLMs. Although these tests provide a convenient and fully automated way to score aspects of "creativity," their validity as measures of machine creativity has not been established. To address this problem, we conduct the first large-scale, systematic study assessing the effectiveness of semantic distance tests for predicting the creative achievement of LLMs across four target constructs: (a) creative writing, (b) output diversity on open-ended prompts, (c) combinatorial creativity, and (d) scientific ideation. We score each test on two criteria (validity and specificity), and derive a theoretical limit for the maximum attainable specificity and validity a test can achieve. We find that: (1) No test is a significant predictor of output diversity, suggesting that point creativity, the ability to produce a single response connecting semantically distant concepts, and distributional creativity, the ability to produce distinct responses across repeated samples, may dissociate in current LLMs--a pattern we call jagged creativity. (2) The Remote Associates Test is effectively a proxy for general capabilities rather than a specific predictor of creativity in LLMs. (3) Lastly, the Divergent Association Task is the best predictor of creative writing, but no single test predicts all constructs well. In summary, our results prescribe caution when applying psychometric tests and tasks of creativity validated among human populations to LLMs.

data.title: CRANE: Constrained Reasoning Injection for Code Agents via Nullspace Editing
data.author: Mingzhi Zhu, Michele Merler, Raju Pavuluri, Stacy Patterson
data.summary: Code agents must both reason over long-horizon repository state and obey strict tool-use protocols. In paired Instruct/Thinking checkpoints, these capabilities are complementary but misaligned. The Instruct model is concise and tool-disciplined, whereas the Thinking model offers stronger planning and recovery behavior but often over-deliberates and degrades agent performance. We present CRANE (Constrained Reasoning Injection for Code Agents via Nullspace Editing), a training-free parameter-editing method that treats the Thinking-Instruct delta as a directional pool of candidate reasoning edits for the Instruct backbone. CRANE combines magnitude thresholding to denoise the delta, a Conservative Taylor Gate to retain edits that are jointly beneficial for reasoning transfer and tool-use preservation, and Graduated Sigmoidal Projection to suppress format-critical update directions. By merging paired Instruct and Thinking checkpoints, CRANE delivers strong gains over either individual model while preserving Instruct-level efficiency: on Roo-Eval it achieves pass1 of 66.2% (+19.5%) for Qwen3-30B-A3B and 81.5% (+8.7%) for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B; on SWE-bench-Verified it resolves up to 14 additional instances at both scales (122/500 and 180/500); and on Terminal-Bench v2 it improves pass1/pass5 by up to 2.3%/7.8%, reaching 7.6%/17.9% and 14.8%/30.3%, respectively, consistently outperforming alternative merging strategies across all three benchmarks.

data.title: Pause and Reflect: Conformal Aggregation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
data.author: Yu Gu, Zijun Yu, Vahid Partovi Nia, Masoud Asgharian
data.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with self-consistency improves performance by aggregating multiple sampled reasoning paths. In this setting, correctness is no longer tied to a single reasoning trace but to the aggregation rule over a pool of candidate paths, making aggregation uncertainty the central challenge. This issue is critical where confidently incorrect answers are far more costly than abstentions. We introduce a conformal procedure for CoT reasoning that directly addresses aggregation uncertainty. Our approach replaces majority voting with weighted score aggregation over reasoning paths and calibrates an abstention rule using conformal risk control. This approach leads to finite-sample guarantees on the confident-error rate--the probability that the system answers and is wrong. We further identify score separability as the key condition under which abstention provably improves selective accuracy, and derive closed-form expressions that predict accuracy gains from calibration data alone. The method is fully inference-time, and requires no retraining. Across four benchmarks, four open-source models, and three score classes, realized confident-error rates are consistent with the prescribed targets up to calibration-split and test-set variability. Our method achieves $90.1\%$ selective accuracy on GSM8K by abstaining on fewer than $5\%$ of problems, compared with $82.3\%$ accuracy under majority voting and $87.4\%$ under score-weighted voting without abstention, while conformal risk control keeps the expected rate of confidently wrong answers below $10\%$.

oai:arXiv.org:2605.14098v2.label: Pause and Reflect: Conformal Aggregation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

data.title: What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning?
data.author: Andr\'e G. Viveiros, Nuno Gon\c{c}alves, Andr\'e F. T. Martins, Matthias Lindemann
data.summary: Humans can approach complex visual problems by mentally simulating intermediate visual steps, rather than reasoning through language alone. Inspired by this, several works on Vision-Language Models have recently explored chain-of-thought reasoning with continuous latent tokens as intermediate visual imagination steps. In this work, we investigate how recent models leverage such latent tokens. Surprisingly, we find that model accuracy is unaffected when latent tokens are replaced by uninformative dummy tokens. This indicates that latent tokens play a minimal causal role in the model's final prediction. To better understand this phenomenon, we analyze both the training signal provided by oracle latent representations and the quality of the latent tokens generated at inference time. Our experiments reveal two crucial issues holding back latent visual reasoning: First, in most existing datasets, oracle latent tokens provide limited additional information beyond the original image and do not substantially simplify the task, leading models to ignore them during training and effectively bypassing them at inference time. When fine-tuned on a diagnostic dataset, in which latent tokens provide sufficient support for the final prediction, we show that models can causally rely on them. Second, the latent tokens produced at inference time deviate from their corresponding oracle representations, collapsing to a narrow region and preventing benefits even when the model relies on them. Overall, our findings suggest that future progress in latent visual reasoning depends on two key pillars: high-quality datasets with informative intermediate steps and more precise latent token prediction.

data.title: Your Agents Are Aging Too: Agent Lifespan Engineering for Deployed Systems
data.author: Jianing Zhu, Yeonju Ro, John Robertson, Kevin Wang, Junbo Li, Haris Vikalo, Aditya Akella, Zhangyang Wang
data.summary: Long-lived AI agents are increasingly deployed as persistent operational systems, yet they are still mostly evaluated like freshly initialized models. Day-one benchmarks miss a basic systems question: how does an agent's reliability change after deployment? Even when model weights are frozen, an agent's effective state keeps changing as it compresses interaction history, retrieves from a growing memory store, revises facts after updates, and undergoes routine maintenance. Reliability therefore becomes a lifespan property of the full agent harness, not only a snapshot property of the base model. We introduce AgingBench, a longitudinal reliability benchmark for agent lifespan engineering: measuring not only whether deployed agents degrade, but what form the degradation takes and where repair should target. AgingBench organizes agent aging into four mechanisms: compression aging, where writing and rewriting drops future-relevant details; interference aging, where accumulated similar memories crowd out the target fact; revision aging, where changed or derived state is not updated correctly; and maintenance aging, where lifecycle events such as model swapping trigger regressions. To diagnose these failures, AgingBench uses temporal dependency graphs and counterfactual probes that produce diagnostic profiles for the write, retrieval, and utilization stages of the memory pipeline. Across 6 scenarios, 10 memory systems and 6 models from two families, we find that agent aging is not one-dimensional over 400 runs spanning 50-200 sessions: a well-formed reply can hide a value the memory no longer supplies; derived state collapses as updates accumulate; and the same wrong answer can require different repairs depending on what the diagnostic profile points to.

oai:arXiv.org:2605.26302v2.label: Your Agents Are Aging Too: Agent Lifespan Engineering for Deployed Systems

data.title: Knowing When to Ask: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for LLM Tool Use
data.author: Abhijit Kumar, Zoey Wu, Mohit Suley
data.summary: Humans know when to reach for help e.g. $347 \times 28$ warrants a calculator while $2+2$ does not. Language models do not. Prompt-based approaches can instruct a model when to invoke tools, but this scaffolding does not teach it to recognize the boundary of its own knowledge. RL approaches that assign a single outcome reward to the whole trajectory fare no better: trajectory-level credit cannot isolate which tool call in a successful episode actually helped, nor penalize unnecessary calls. We propose CARL (Competence-Aware Reinforcement Learning), which trains a critic on the model's own rollouts to learn where parametric knowledge suffices and where it needs external help. By decomposing each rollout at natural tool-use boundaries (e.g., code fence delimiters and context block transitions), CARL assigns independent credit to each segment from a single binary outcome, without external judges or step-level annotations. As a result, erroneous tool calls, incorrect extractions, and unnecessary calls each receive appropriately signed advantages. The trained critic captures the model's domain competence: it separates parametrically solvable from tool-dependent questions with AUC 0.93 at 7B. On five benchmarks spanning arithmetic, multi-hop factual QA, and numerical reasoning over financial tables, CARL improves average exact-match accuracy on the three search benchmarks by 6.7 points at 7B and 9.6 points at 3B over the best RL baseline, with the largest gain (+8.3 EM at 7B, +12.5 EM at 3B) on MuSiQue. At 7B, CARL has a 53% lower tool-use rate than Search-R1 PPO on parametrically answerable questions while remaining 9.8 EM points more accurate on them. Gains are largest at small scale: the 3B improvement is $1.4\times$ the 7B improvement, suggesting that knowing when to ask disproportionately benefits models with smaller parametric memory.

data.title: Token Inflation: How Dishonest Providers Can Overcharge for Large Language Model Usage
data.author: Shahinul Hoque, Jinghuai Zhang, Jinyuan Sun, Fnu Suya
data.summary: Per-token billing is now the standard pricing model for commercial large language models (LLMs), so the honesty of reported token counts directly affects what users pay. We show that this kind of billing is hard to audit by design: providers hide the model, the tokenizer, and the execution to protect their IP, mitigate jailbreaks, and preserve user privacy, which means an auditor can only inspect proofs the provider supplies. The audit therefore reduces to a consistency check on the provider's own reports. We call this a trust paradox: every audit must trust some artifact, but current frameworks trust exactly the ones a provider has the strongest reason to manipulate. We study three recent token auditing frameworks and show that a provider with ordinary commercial capabilities can systematically inflate billed token counts. In the most permissive setting, hidden reasoning usage can be inflated by 1,469% on average without detection. At current frontier reasoning prices, that turns a \$100 honest bill into roughly a \$1,569 bill on the same query. Even when the user can see the full reasoning string, tokenization ambiguity alone still allows 50.85% over-reporting below the detection threshold. These results suggest the problem is not in any specific auditor but in any audit whose evidence comes from the audited party. Restoring honest billing will require verification that ties reported token counts to evidence the provider does not control, such as trusted execution attestation, cryptographic proofs of inference, or third-party re-execution.

oai:arXiv.org:2605.30040v2.label: Token Inflation: How Dishonest Providers Can Overcharge for Large Language Model Usage

data.title: PithTrain: A Compact and Agent-Native MoE Training System
data.author: Ruihang Lai, Hao Kang, Haozhan Tang, Akaash R. Parthasarathy, Zichun Yu, Junru Shao, Todd C. Mowry, Chenyan Xiong, Tianqi Chen
data.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the dominant architecture for frontier language models. To meet this demand, production frameworks have built optimized MoE training stacks over years of engineering effort. Yet evolving these stacks for new architectures and system optimizations remains expensive. With the rise of AI coding agents, they could automate parts of training-framework development and accelerate this evolution. But applying them to these existing frameworks carries hidden costs, invisible to today's throughput-only evaluations. We name this missing dimension agent-task efficiency (ATE): the cost of using coding agents to understand, operate, and extend a framework. Grounded in four agent-native design principles, we build PithTrain, a compact, agent-native MoE training framework supporting pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. We further introduce ATE-Bench, covering real-world training-framework tasks. Our evaluation shows PithTrain achieves throughput competitive with production frameworks and higher agent-task efficiency on ATE-Bench. On new-feature tasks, PithTrain uses up to 62% fewer Agent Turns than Megatron-LM, and up to 44% and 64% less Active GPU Time than Megatron-LM and TorchTitan, respectively.

data.title: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
data.author: Alessio Bruno
data.summary: We present Moxia, a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for self-explaining mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form handler: 5,741 routes, 75.9% of which answer without invoking the model, with zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived, so is its explanation, rendered from the steps the handler took; where the derivation fits a fragment of Lean 4 with Mathlib, the same declared data become a theorem the kernel checks. On the full 5,000-record MATH test split, designed against, Moxia answers 95.6% (4,780/5,000) with zero confident-wrong answers and abstains, saying where, on the other 220; its MATH-500 subset reads 95.2% (476/500), also with zero wrong. Earlier versions called MATH-500 held out; it is a subset of the test split, and this version says so. We release the run record by record: the problem, the expected answer, the model's transcription, the answer or abstention, the explanation, and the Lean theorem marked as compiled. 3,142 of the 4,780 correct answers carry a theorem, and all 3,142 compile; building the theorems actually served, not only a fixture corpus, found seven that did not, two of them false statements beside correct answers, all repaired before release. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry.

data.title: An Enigma of Artificial Reason: Investigating the Production-Evaluation Gap in Large Reasoning Models
data.author: Mingzhong Sun, Teresa Yeo, Armando Solar-Lezama, Tan Zhi-Xuan
data.summary:
Studies of human reasoning have shown that people are typically stronger at evaluating reasoning than producing it from scratch. In contrast, large reasoning models (LRMs) are trained to excel at producing long chains of reasoning to solve complex problems. How then do LRMs perform at evaluating reasons? We investigate this with the Valid-Answer-Invalid-Reasoning (VAIR) dataset: math problems and solutions with trivial reasoning flaws but valid answers, designed to isolate reasoning evaluation from the confound of reasoning production. Unlike humans, who we find are only 6% worse at grading than solving such problems, we find a substantial production-evaluation gap in LRMs: frontier models score as low as 52% when evaluating VAIR solutions, despite near-perfect solution production.
Why this enigma? Through chain-of-thought (CoT) analysis, we find evidence of an answer confirmation bias: LRMs often produce then check for the correct answer instead of carefully verifying each step, fabricating rationalizations even when noticing anomalous reasoning. Linear probes corroborate this, showing that while LRM activations encode some representation of valid reasoning, they fail to robustly represent VAIR solutions as invalid. Causal patching of the final answer's representations causes LRM verdicts and activations to flip at substantial rates, demonstrating that answer validity is a causal factor in models' confirmation biases. These findings indicate an outstanding limitation in dominant approaches to reasoning training, which incentivize LRMs to produce and confirm reasoning towards correct answers, but not to robustly evaluate the underlying reasons

data.title: PersonaDrive: Human-Style Retrieval-Augmented VLA Agents for Closed-Loop Driving Simulation
data.author: Mahmoud Srewa, Praneetsai Vasu Iddamsetty, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Salma Elmalaki
data.summary: Closed-loop driving simulators mostly fill their environments with traffic agents that behave alike, whether they are rule-based or learned. Recent methods that control driving style learn it from labels inferred from existing driving recordings, from synthetic data generated to reflect each style, or from reward weights estimated by a large language model (LLM). All of these are indirect estimates of a style, not recordings of people who were instructed to drive in it. We introduce PersonaDrive, a vision-language-action (VLA) driving agent that takes its style from retrieved human demonstrations. The demonstrations come from a new dataset in which 15 participants drove CARLA routes on a driving simulator under conservative, neutral, and aggressive instructions. PersonaDrive trains a lightweight retrieval head on features from a frozen image encoder and on control signals over per-style databases, and fine-tunes one VLA backbone over the retrieved demonstrations. Switching style only means searching a different FAISS index, with no retraining. On the Bench2Drive benchmark without style conditioning, PersonaDrive improves the Driving Score by 4.6% over SimLingo and by 2.5% over HiP-AD, a gain that fine-tuning without retrieval does not reproduce. With style conditioning, PersonaDrive outperforms the strongest baseline, Drive My Way, in every style, with a Driving Score 6.7% to 11.6% higher. Its driving also follows the instruction, since average speed rises by 19.8% from the conservative to the aggressive style. Each traffic agent is evaluated individually as a driving policy. The dataset and model weights are available on the project page: https://pervasiveautonomylab.github.io/personadrive-landpage/.

oai:arXiv.org:2606.12616v2.label: PersonaDrive: Human-Style Retrieval-Augmented VLA Agents for Closed-Loop Driving Simulation

data.title: Animation2Code: Evaluating Temporal Visual Reasoning in Video-to-Code Generation
data.author: Anya Ji, Abhijith Varma Mudunuri, David M. Chan, Alane Suhr
data.summary: While recent vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved significant improvements on static visual-to-code tasks such as generating code for webpages, charts, or SVGs, it remains unclear whether they can recover temporal dynamics when motion is present. To this end, we introduce Animation2Code, a benchmark for evaluating temporal visual reasoning via reconstructing executable web animation code from videos. Animation2Code consists of 1,069 web animation videos with diverse visual appearances and motion patterns, paired with corresponding HTML/CSS/JavaScript implementations. We propose two human-aligned metrics, appearance similarity and temporal similarity, which allow us to disentangle visual fidelity from temporal alignment when comparing rendered animations against ground-truth samples. Benchmarking state-of-the-art VLMs on this dataset shows that current VLMs struggle to maintain temporal consistency in reconstruction, even when achieving high appearance similarity, including under finetuning and iterative refinement settings. Code and data are available at https://anya-ji.github.io/animation2code-website .

oai:arXiv.org:2606.28593v2.label: Animation2Code: Evaluating Temporal Visual Reasoning in Video-to-Code Generation

data.title: PolicyGuard: A Dialogue-Grounded Sub-Agent Verifier for Policy Adherence in LLM Agents
data.author: Seongjae Kang, Taehyung Yu, Sung Ju Hwang
data.summary: LLM agents handle user requests on behalf of organizations through tool calls and must follow the company policies stated in their system prompts. Prior work approaches this as a safeguarding problem -- external checks that block non-compliant agent actions. We argue that policy adherence is broader: real workflows unfold across many turns, require explicit user confirmation and prerequisite reads, and hinge on dialogue rather than on any single argument value. We introduce PolicyGuard, a sub-agent verifier that shares the agent's view of the dialogue, reasons over the policy in context, and returns actionable remediation. On $\tau^2$-bench airline across GPT 5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 2.5 Pro, PolicyGuard improves $\mathrm{Pass}^4$, the fraction of tasks successful in all four trials, by +12.0 / +6.0 / +12.0 pp; pooled paired tests support an overall cross-vendor effect. We further evaluate PolicyGuard on the full retail and telecom base splits, covering all three $\tau^2$-bench customer-service domains. Further analyses show that PolicyGuard improves reliability beyond agent self-checking, catches more policy violations with fewer blocks than argument-level guards, and preserves its refusal accuracy under three adversarial probes.

oai:arXiv.org:2606.29225v2.label: PolicyGuard: A Dialogue-Grounded Sub-Agent Verifier for Policy Adherence in LLM Agents

data.title: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction
data.author: Gaoxiang Luo, Yifan Wu, Sinian Zhang, Aryan Deshwal, Ju Sun
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as critical decision-making components in high-stakes real-world AI systems, rendering LLM reliability a foremost practical concern. In this paper, we focus on enhancing LLM reliability through selective prediction (SP), a strategy that allows an LLM to only predict for inputs where it is likely to be correct (i.e., coverage) and hence reduce the error rate (i.e., risk) on that portion of inputs---flagging the remaining inputs for future human discretion. In other words, SP improves LLM reliability by balancing the risk-coverage trade-off and enabling seamless human-AI collaboration. To integrate SP into LLMs, we focus on the LLM post-training alignment stage and propose to align LLMs with SP performance metrics, in contrast with existing LLM alignment methods that focus primarily on correctness or calibration metrics. Specifically, we propose a novel alignment framework, Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward (RLSR), which targets the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC)---a popular SP performance metric---as its alignment objective. RLSR achieves substantially better risk-coverage trade-off compared to multiple alignment baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.

oai:arXiv.org:2607.03528v2.label: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction

data.title: LLM Watermarking as Big Data Provenance: A Deployment-Oriented Systematization
data.author: Huy Phan, Kieu Dang, Ojaswi Dulal, Aiham AL Shukairi, Abby Shine, Chase Garner, Phung Lai
data.summary: As large language models (LLMs) generate and transform content at scale, reliable attribution becomes an increasingly important requirement for big data provenance. Although numerous watermarking methods have been proposed, existing evaluations predominantly emphasize sample-level detectability and robustness, leaving deployment requirements such as serving efficiency, population-scale false positives, multi-key attribution, and long-term verification less systematically examined. This paper presents a deployment-oriented systematization of LLM watermarking through the five Vs of big data: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, and Value. We classify representative watermarking methods across four dimensions: insertion point, verification authority, operational state, and adversarial threat model. We further map these methods to four deployment workloads: online generation, streaming detection, transformation pipelines, and ecosystem governance. Our synthesis identifies recurring limitations, including dependencies on generation-time access, additional inference overhead, sensitivity to downstream transformations, and incomplete reporting of calibration and lifecycle compatibility. Based on these findings, we propose workload-specific evaluation requirements covering statistical reliability, throughput, utility, robustness, and governance. This framework connects watermark design choices to practical deployment constraints and provides guidance for selecting and evaluating provenance mechanisms in large-scale data ecosystems.

oai:arXiv.org:2607.10103v3.label: LLM Watermarking as Big Data Provenance: A Deployment-Oriented Systematization

data.title: SlotGuard: Stop Oversharing Private Local Context in LLM Agent Transcripts
data.author: Haocheng Xia, Yongjoo Park
data.summary: LLM agents can expose private local context (e.g., paths, emails) and credentials (e.g., API keys) as agent observations (e.g., tool outputs, shell logs, and file reads) are appended to provider-bound transcripts. Existing placeholder redaction is brittle: it can miss embedded or cross-turn references, over-redact benign lookalikes, and destroy the structure useful for reasoning. We present SlotGuard, a local transcript boundary that can hide sensitive data while retaining agents' performance. SlotGuard rewrites structural bindings as typed, suffix-aware slots, replaces secrets with format-preserving synthetic values, links cross-turn references with a lightweight session graph, and restores raw values only inside the trusted runtime. On controlled repository-oriented agent transcripts, SlotGuard removes all 20,814 annotated structurally sensitive characters across 9,229 paths and reduces credential leakage to 0.0% across 852 planted values. It remains close to raw-transcript task success across four upstream models, while generic redaction drops to 2.5%. Deterministic transcript rewriting takes a median of 14.424 microseconds per agent turn, excluding the optional semantic detector. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/illinoisdata/SlotGuard.

oai:arXiv.org:2607.17147v2.label: SlotGuard: Stop Oversharing Private Local Context in LLM Agent Transcripts

data.title: ClinFusion: A Vision-Centric Multimodal LLM System for Holistic Medical Understanding
data.author: Hangjie Yuan, Yichen Qian, Zhiwei Tang, Xianzhe Xu, Sicheng Yang, Lirong Wu, Jinwang Wang, Pengju Wang, Zhitao Zeng, Yizeng Han, Yan Xing, Shengxuan Luo, Tao Feng, Qing Xie, Weigen Yao, Yi Yang, Zuozhu Liu, Jiasheng Tang, Xiaomao Yu, Shaocheng Wang, Jitao Wang, Jiahong Dong, Weihua Chen, Feng Xu, Fan Wang
data.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) hold immense potential to revolutionize clinical practice, yet deploying them in the medical domain is fundamentally a vision-centric challenge: models must absorb knowledge from heterogeneous 2D and 3D medical images, and evaluation protocols must align with radiologists' clinical practice and provide an accurate, fine-grained and factualness-driven assessment. In this paper, we introduce ClinFusion, a vision-centric MLLM designed for holistic medical understanding that systematically addresses these limitations. We propose a compositional and cascaded vision encoder architecture featuring a Cascade Spatial-Aware Locality Fusion operator that unifies diverse 2D and native 3D medical image understanding within a fused encoder. We further introduce a vision-grounded evaluation framework, including MedIF-Bench for instruction-following assessment and a region-of-interest-grounded method for clinically aligned and factualness-driven report generation evaluation. We show that ClinFusion sets a new state-of-the-art across a comprehensive suite of 2D and 3D multimodal medical benchmarks---spanning visual question answering, report generation, and instruction following---as well as textual medical tasks, outperforming leading open-source medical MLLMs (\textit{e.g.}, Hulu-Med, Lingshu) on 20 out of 24 benchmarks and demonstrating multimodal capabilities better than powerful proprietary models such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash on 13 out of 16 benchmarks, and can be further augmented with agentic tool use for retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted clinical workflows. A blinded evaluation by board-certified radiologists confirms that ClinFusion produces the highest-ranked reports, and validates our RoI-grounded metric as achieving the strongest correlation with expert judgment among all automatic evaluation metrics examined.

oai:arXiv.org:2607.24743v4.label: ClinFusion: A Vision-Centric Multimodal LLM System for Holistic Medical Understanding

data.title: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents
data.author: Seongjae Kang, Taehyung Yu, Sung Ju Hwang
data.summary: Customer-service LLM agents must follow organizational policy when acting on a user's behalf. Compliance failures arise from either forbidden actions, such as granting an ineligible change, or omitted procedural requirements, such as identification or confirmation. Runtime safeguards can intervene on risky actions, but action-local checks do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. Workflow-following systems support prescribed process execution, but primarily target workflow completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior. PolicyGuide instead compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. From persisted graph state, the verifier reconciles open requests and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Across the $\tau^2$-bench airline, retail, and telecom domains with a GPT 5.4 agent and verifier, PolicyGuide raises mean $\mathrm{Pass}^4$ from $0.42$ to $0.62$, with the largest gain on telecom ($0.19$ to $0.61$), the most workflow-structured domain. The same workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Complementary evaluations find the lowest observed attack-success rate under adversarial users and the strongest procedural compliance in an independently validated workflow-level audit.

oai:arXiv.org:2608.19861v2.label: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents

data.title: LLMs as Adaptive Meta-Solvers: Strategy-Diverse RL for Industrial-Scale Optimization
data.author: Shihao Zhang, Weiting Liu, Siyu Shao, Yitian Chen, Jianfeng Feng, Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye
data.summary: Scaling LLM-based optimization from textbook-scale instances to real-world, industrial tasks remains a critical open challenge. Existing approaches are predominantly evaluated on small, self-contained textual problems and often commit to a solver-integrated paradigm, limiting their ability to handle the scale and structural diversity of practical optimization workloads. In this work, we propose a practical framework for training open-source LLMs to tackle real-world, industrial-scale optimization. We first show empirically that solver-integrated reasoning, exact combinatorial algorithm, and heuristic search exhibit complementary strengths across different problem structures and scales. Motivated by this, we introduce Strategy-Diverse Reinforcement Learning (SDRL), which trains LLMs as adaptive optimization meta-solvers. SDRL leverages this complementarity through a correctness-gated hierarchical diversity reward that promotes robust exploration across varying strategies and within each strategy, effectively preventing premature strategy collapse. We further introduce a mixed-format training scheme that jointly supports both self-contained textual problems and file-grounded instances. Across comprehensive evaluations, our framework outperforms existing fine-tuned methods and frontier models including DeepSeek-V4-Pro and GPT-5.5, both on average across benchmarks and on industrial-scale optimization tasks. We release our code and training data to facilitate future research https://github.com/tokentideAI/LLMMetaSolver.

oai:arXiv.org:2609.34427v2.label: LLMs as Adaptive Meta-Solvers: Strategy-Diverse RL for Industrial-Scale Optimization

data.title: VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation
data.author: Hanxun Huang, Yutao Wu, Qizhou Wang, Silvia Monta\~na-Ni\~no, Yige Li, Xiang Zheng, Elif Buse Doyuran, Phoebe Matich, Xiao Liu, Xingjun Ma, Sarah Erfani, Christopher Leckie
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have made misinformation inexpensive to produce but not to verify, creating a growing asymmetry in the information ecosystem. Under tight time, labor, and budget constraints, media organizations, platforms, and fact-checkers rely on screening to prioritize which content to verify. We introduce VEX-Bench, a unified benchmark for evaluating the verification complexity of LLM-generated misinformation, as perceived during screening, across models and generation methods. Verification complexity is assessed along multiple dimensions derived from journalistic and fact-checking practices, capturing checkability, harm potential, source credibility signals, imposter legitimacy, and expected verification effort. We define the VEX score as an integrated measure combining elicitation yield and verification complexity to quantify how generated content consumes limited verification capacity. We construct a benchmark spanning two misinformation categories, 6 high-stakes domains, and 60 real-world topics, and evaluate 7 frontier LLMs and 7 generation methods, yielding 5{,}880 articles. We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $\alpha$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. LLMs can generate high-VEX misinformation at 3$\times$ to 169$\times$ lower cost than agent-based verification. Such content is often prioritized during screening, consuming scarce verification resources and introducing a systematic risk of misallocation in resource-constrained verification systems. The code is publicly available in our \href{https://github.com/HanxunH/VEX-Bench}{GitHub repository}.

data.title: Typed Edge-Tensor Non-Reciprocal Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning
data.author: Zeyu Jia
data.summary: Scaling test-time computation in continuous latent spaces offers an attractive alternative to verbose token-by-token generation for multi-step deductive reasoning. However, unregularized recurrent latent updates suffer from a deliberation drift cliff when rolled out beyond training horizons, while strictly energy-conserving or symmetric message-passing dynamics cannot break parent-to-child causal symmetry or suppress cyclic modus-ponens amplification on cyclic distraction graphs. We introduce Typed Edge-Tensor Non-Reciprocal Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation (TE-BPHD), a neuro-symbolic continuous-time latent reasoning architecture that couples skew-symmetric port-Hamiltonian conservation with relation-typed non-reciprocal directional transport and monotone dissipative damping on a semantic entity-state manifold. We prove (i) unconditional input-to-state stability and exponential contraction of autonomous rollouts across arbitrary inference depths without external norm projection, (ii) strict directional DAG reachability separation over symmetric message passing, and (iii) exact cycle-suppression margins under finite cyclic horn perturbations. Across counterfactual open-world deductive benchmarks (PrOntoQA-OOD up to depth 15, ProofWriter-OWA Cyclic at depths 5-10, FOLIO-Symbolic, and Cluttr-Relational), TE-BPHD eliminates the deep-horizon drift cliff, improves depth-10 cyclic reasoning accuracy to 90.0% (+/- 0.8%) over symmetric port-Hamiltonian and standard Transformer baselines, and supports zero-retraining adaptive Lyapunov halting that reduces average solver evaluations by 44% with negligible accuracy loss.

data.title: What Does a Harness Repair? Four Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model
data.author: Bowen Xu, Boyu Chen
data.summary: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit traced its gain to rows the start left unparsed and found that the caller sent reference answers as assistant turns; replication through the same pipeline missed this defect. We preregistered four studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over capped thinking in 7 of 12 cells, mainly by parsing rows the cap left unparsed, and was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells. Replication reproduced an injected defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases. At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 test points but were not detectably above the strongest constant label. In the third study, GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory), thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed; the fourth comparison was inconclusive on test. On exploratory Autocast, harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers on test. On the prediction tasks (14B mortality, Autocast) the harnesses ended near the constant label. The fourth study varied search-set skew and objective on CREAK and resolved Manifold questions. All its results are descriptive because render hashes were not committed before the first replication call (D001). Minority-recall estimates were lower at 80:20 than at 50:50 in all four test cells. The balanced objective and re-selection from each search's pool had higher minority- and lower majority-recall estimates in all four cells. Five of their eight minority-recall intervals included zero, as did all eight balanced-accuracy contrast intervals. This does not show that skew explains the earlier collapse.
